You ask for and give directions in town; you use the imperative (gira, giri), articulated prepositions (al, nel, sul, dal) and the verbs VENIRE and USCIRE.
Excuse me, where is the Ponte Vecchio?
Go straight on and then turn right.
The pharmacy is next to the church.
The book is on the table.
Are you coming with me tonight?
To ask politely where a place is and whether it's far.
To understand and give directions: dritto, a destra, a sinistra, attraversare.
To use the imperative with "tu" (gira!) and with "Lei" (giri!).
To use articulated prepositions: al, allo, alla, nel, nella, sul, dal, del.
To conjugate the irregular verbs VENIRE and USCIRE.
To describe where something is: vicino a, davanti a, accanto a, tra.
Saturday morning, on Ponte Santa Trinita. Matei is on his way to the market when a tourist couple with a map stops him.
Excuse me, are you from here? Where is the basilica of Santa Croce?
I'm not from here, but I live in Florence. Santa Croce is a bit far.
Is it far? Can we walk?
Yes, it's twenty minutes. Cross the bridge and keep going straight until you reach the river.
Then turn right and walk along the Arno. After the Ponte Vecchio, take the second street on the left.
The second on the left. And the basilica?
The basilica is in the big square, right in front of you. You can't miss it: it's white and green.
Is there a bar nearby? My husband is hungry.
Yes, there are lots of bars in the square. But watch the prices!
Thank you very much! Where are you from?
I'm Romanian. I come from Sibiu.
A Romanian explaining Florence to tourists! How lovely!
Florence belongs to everyone. Have a nice day!
GI is read as in Romanian: "giri" = "jee-ri", not "ghee-ri". Likewise: girare, giardino.
"Scusi" has SC + u = "sk": SKU-zi. But "uscire" has SC + i = "sh": u-SHI-re, esce = "e-she".
"Chiesa" = "kye-za", with CH = "k". Be careful not to say "chee-sa".
Some words are stressed on the third syllable from the end: se-MA-fo-ro, ba-SI-li-ca. Others on the second-to-last: fer-MA-ta. Listen and repeat.
Scusi, c'è una farmacia qui vicino?
Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?
How do I get to the Duomo?
Is it far? / Is it near?
How long does it take on foot?
"Dov'è" = "dove è" contracted. In the plural: "Dove sono i bagni?" (Where are the toilets?).
With "tu", the imperative of -ARE verbs ends in -A, and of -ERE / -IRE verbs in -I. With "Lei" (polite), the endings swap: -ARE → -I, -ERE / -IRE → -A.
Now you understand why you say "scusi" to a stranger and "scusa" to a friend: it's the same imperative, with "Lei" and with "tu".
The negative with "tu" is "non" + infinitive: "Non girare!" (Don't turn!). With "Lei": "Non giri!".
The prepositions a, da, di, in, su merge with the definite article. It looks complicated, but it's logical:
The keys are in the bag.
"Con" and "per" don't merge (in modern Italian): con il, per la.
tra la banca e il bar
"Vicino a" and "lontano da" take different prepositions: vicino AL centro, but lontano DAL centro.
Are you coming to the cinema with me?
Tonight we're going out with friends.
"Uscire" also means "to go out (in the evening)": "Esci stasera?" = "Are you going out tonight?".
Signora, turn left at the traffic lights.
The cat is on the sofa.
Tonight I'm going out with Giulia.
What do you say to a friend to get past?
Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?
Dopo il Ponte Vecchio, quale strada devono prendere?
Di che colore è la basilica?
Perché il marito vuole un bar?
On Wednesday afternoon Pietro comes to Matei's with a big sheet of paper and a pencil. "Today we're making a treasure map of the Oltrarno," he says. "You're new: this way you'll learn the streets."
Pietro first draws his grandmother's trattoria, on via Maggio. "This is the base," he explains. "From here you go out and turn right."
Then he draws Piazza Santo Spirito, with the church and the fountain. "Next to the church there's Giulia's bar. In front of the fountain, on Saturdays, there's the market."
After the square, Pietro draws a narrow little street. "Here's Signor Franco's shop. He sells old wooden toys. It's not far from school."
"And where's the treasure?" Matei asks. Pietro smiles and draws a big X between the bridge and the Boboli gardens.
"Here. But you have to find it yourself. Follow the map: go straight, cross the street, turn left after the pharmacy."
On Saturday morning Matei goes out with the map in his pocket. He goes straight, crosses, turns left after the pharmacy. And he arrives in front of a tiny ice-cream shop.
On the door there's a note written by Pietro: "The treasure is the pistachio ice cream. The best in Florence. Your treat!" Behind the door, with two cones in his hands, is Pietro.
Che cosa vende il signor Franco?
The bar is between the pharmacy and the church.
Is it far from the centre?
